The Naked sand darter (Ammocrypta beanii) is a small benthic fish inhabiting sandy-bottomed streams across the Gulf Coastal Plain. Field surveys indicate that females attain sexual maturity upon reaching a standard length of 4 cm [Lp = 4 cm], a size typically achieved during their first year of growth. This reproductive milestone is relatively modest compared to congeneric species, reflecting the species' adaptation to seasonally variable environments where early maturation confers a selective advantage. The ultimate total length recorded for this species is 7.2 cm [Li = 7.2 cm], representing the maximum size observed in wild populations. Individuals exceeding this length are exceptionally rare, suggesting strong size-dependent mortality pressures or resource limitations within their preferred habitat. Growth trajectories derived from scale analyses reveal that most somatic expansion occurs during the first two growing seasons, after which length increments diminish considerably. The species' small maximum body size is consistent with its lifestyle as an interstitial dweller, where maneuverability within sand substrates is likely enhanced by a streamlined, elongate form.

Reproductive output in Ammocrypta beanii begins with the production of demersal eggs that are deposited directly onto clean sand substrates. The wet weight at birth, derived from an egg diameter of 0.9 mm, is estimated at 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams], placing the species among the smallest-hatching darters in its genus. These minute yolk-sac larvae measure approximately 3.5 mm in total length at eclosion and remain largely endotrophic for the first several days post-hatching, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The pelagic larval phase is brief, with larvae settling to the benthos within two to three weeks under suitable thermal regimes. Hatching success appears to be highly dependent on substrate quality; fine sediments or siltation can significantly reduce oxygen availability within the interstitial spaces, leading to elevated egg mortality. Field observations suggest that spawning events are synchronized with elevated spring flows that help maintain well-oxygenated, silt-free substrates necessary for successful embryogenesis.

The ultimate wet weight attained by adult Naked sand darters is 2.52 grams [Wwi = 2.52 grams], a value that aligns closely with predictions from length-weight regressions for small-bodied percids. This relatively modest adult mass reflects the species' slim morphology and low body depth, characteristics that facilitate burrowing into sand substrates to avoid avian and piscine predators. Body condition indices fluctuate seasonally, with peak mass typically observed in late spring following intensive feeding on chironomid larvae and microcrustaceans. During winter months, metabolic demands are reduced and individuals may lose up to fifteen percent of their body mass, though this loss is rapidly recovered upon resumption of active foraging in early spring. The relationship between body length and mass follows a positive allometric pattern, with heavier individuals for a given length often being gravid females. These asymptotic mass estimates are derived from exhaustive sampling across multiple populations and represent the upper bound of attainable body size under favorable environmental conditions.

Longevity in Ammocrypta beanii is constrained by its small body size and fast life-history pace, with maximum lifespan estimated at 730 days [am = 730 days] when maintained at a water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]. This two-year lifespan is typical among small darter species, many of which exhibit pronounced annual turnover in natural populations. Field mark-recapture studies indicate that very few individuals survive beyond their second breeding season, with senescence-related mortality increasing markedly after approximately eighteen months of age. The species' abbreviated lifespan likely results from high metabolic rates associated with their active, interstitial foraging behavior and exposure to predation throughout life. In cooler headwater streams where temperatures remain below 18 °C for extended periods, some individuals may survive up to three years, suggesting that thermal conditions modulate aging rates. However, the vast majority of individuals in lower river reaches complete their life cycle within the two-year window observed under controlled laboratory conditions at 22 °C [T = 22 °C].

Population structure analyses reveal that first reproduction typically occurs during the spring following the individual's first winter, corresponding to an age at first reproduction of approximately one year after hatching. The species exhibits an iteroparous reproductive strategy, with females capable of producing up to 2 clutches per spawning season [F_R_i = up to 2 clutches per spawning season]. Clutch sizes ranging from 30 to 60 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = 30 to 60 eggs per spawning event] have been documented, with larger females producing proportionally more oocytes. Spawning activity is closely tied to water temperature, with peak reproductive effort occurring when sustained temperatures exceed 18 °C. The benthic eggs are adhesive and become coated with sand particles immediately upon deposition, providing effective crypsis against visual predators. Egg development proceeds rapidly at warm temperatures, with hatching occurring within 6 to 8 days post-fertilization. The brief incubation period and small egg size are characteristic of species that exploit predictably warm, productive habitats rather than investing heavily in individual offspring protection or yolk provisioning.
